sections.h2: What do the PVA, clerk and sheriff each do in Marshall County?
sections.html:
Valuation and recording share one address, 1101 Main Street in Benton, where the PVA and the County Clerk keep offices. Collection of the bill belongs to the sheriff.

  • PVA: appraises property and takes exemption filings. The county directory shows 270-527-4767 as an alternate phone, with the office open on weekdays until 4:30.
  • Clerk: holds every land record in the county and, in the county's own description, collects delinquent property taxes. Call 270-527-4740.
  • Sheriff: collects county tax. A bill lookup and payment link sits on the sheriff's page at marshallcountyky.gov.

Tax collection is one job among several for the sheriff, whose deputies patrol about 300 square miles and more than 900 miles of road, work the lake with marine patrols, and provide court security.

A house inside Benton brings a second bill. City Hall, 1009 Main Street (270-527-8677), collects Benton's own property tax, and the city's website cautions residents against using its link for county taxes.

sections.h2: How did Kentucky Lake shape Marshall County real estate?
sections.html:
Water explains most of Marshall County's modern history. The Tennessee River and Kentucky Lake form its northeastern border. Of 340 square miles, 39 are water. It is the only Purchase-region county that does not touch another state.

The legislature split the county from the northern half of Calloway County in 1842. For its first century the economy was farming, and the population swung hard: 15,215 in 1920, 12,889 in 1930, 16,602 in 1940 and 13,387 in 1950. In the 1940s the Tennessee Valley Authority impounded Kentucky Lake. Fishing resorts followed, and low-cost power from Kentucky Dam brought chemical and manufacturing plants to Calvert City. The impoundment flooded Birmingham and Gilbertsville, and Gilbertsville was rebuilt west of its first site. The county then grew to 20,381 by 1970, 25,637 by 1980 and 30,125 by 2000.

Benton, the seat, is the biggest of the county's three cities, with Calvert City and Hardin the others. Gilbertsville is counted as a census-designated place, and Aurora, Draffenville, Fairdealing and Briensburg are unincorporated. A state marker near Benton commemorates a March 23, 1864 clash between Confederate and Union cavalry. Central time applies here, and part of the Clarks River National Wildlife Refuge lies within the county. Owners of lakeside or second-home parcels should ask the PVA for the property's classification and last inspection date.

sections.h2: Who lives in Marshall County, according to the Census?
sections.html:
Marshall County leans older: one resident in four is 65 or over. Owners live in more than four of every five homes.

Housing units outnumber households by roughly 3,800, a gap that reflects vacant and seasonal homes of the kind that line a lake. Ask a local agent how competing listings are counted before you set a price.

The July 2025 estimate of 31,659 equals the 2020 count exactly. Poverty affects 10.7 percent of residents, and about 91 percent of adults finished high school. A bachelor's degree is held by 21.2 percent. Commutes average 23.7 minutes. In 2023 the county's 734 employer establishments employed 9,645 people, paid $600.5 million and added 6.3 percent more jobs than the year before. In 2022, stores sold $638.4 million of goods, health care and social assistance billed $77.9 million, and transportation and warehousing billed $62.8 million. A further 2,366 businesses have no employees. Veterans number 1,879, foreign-born residents are 0.9 percent of the total, and broadband reaches 85.5 percent of households. Density barely moved between 2010 and 2020, from 104.4 to 104.8 people per square mile.

sections.h2: Why were Marshall County's 2026 tax bills mailed late?
sections.html:
Rates had to be finalized before the bills could be printed, so the Sheriff's Office announced a collection start of November 1, as Marshall County Daily reported on October 9, 2026. The schedule it published:

  • November 1 to 30, 2026: two percent discount.
  • December 1 to 31, 2026: face amount due.
  • January 1 to 31, 2027: five percent penalty.
  • February 1 to April 15, 2027: ten percent penalty.

Such a shifted calendar is permitted by KRS 134.015(3), under which the Department of Revenue can swap in new dates when billing falls behind. In a normal year the two percent discount ends November 1, and the face amount is good through December.

Whatever the year, trust the dates printed on your own bill. When the cycle ends, open bills pass to the County Clerk, and the Department of Revenue says they then accrue one percent interest monthly.

sections.h2: Where does a Marshall County owner turn when a value looks too high?
sections.html:
Walk into the PVA's office and ask for a conference, the opening move in KRS 133.120. Still unconvinced? Put your reasons and your own fair-cash-value figure in a petition to the County Clerk no later than one workday after inspection ends, then prepare for the board hearing described in KRS 133.030.

  1. Gather neighborhood sales, an appraisal or construction costs.
  2. Attend yourself, or send someone with written authority.
  3. Keep paying on your own figure until the board decides.

An owner who bypasses the county board loses the later state appeal, so the petition deadline carries weight. Working farmland may qualify for agricultural-use valuation under Section 172A of the state constitution; ask the PVA about it.

sections.h2: Does Marshall County's older population qualify for the homestead exemption?
sections.html: Many do. About one resident in four is 65 or older, so the exemption touches a large share of homes. The $49,100 deduction for 2025 and 2026 turns the median value of $173,800 into $124,700 of taxable assessment. File with the Marshall County PVA, attaching proof of age or a disability classification. The benefit follows the owner, so a qualifying buyer files again.

sections.h2: How do the lien and the deed get handled in a Marshall County sale?
sections.html:
A delinquency lien may remain for eleven years under KRS 134.015(5), so any unpaid year has to be cleared by closing. Because the Marshall County Clerk handles delinquent property tax, prior-year payoffs come from that office (270-527-4740) and the current bill from the sheriff.

Deeds are recorded with the same clerk, who first collects the grantor's transfer tax of fifty cents per $500 of value under KRS 142.050. On a sale at the county median that comes to $174. The clerk lists open hours of 8 AM to 4:30 PM on weekdays, with 270-527-4741 as a second line and 270-527-4746 for the vault. The homepage also promotes protection against deed theft, which any seller should ask about after closing.

faqs.q: Where can I look up my Marshall County tax bill?
faqs.a: Use the bill lookup and payment link on the Sheriff's page of the county website. For value or exemption questions, ask the PVA at 1101 Main Street in Benton.

faqs.q: Do Benton residents pay a separate city property tax?
faqs.a: Yes. The City of Benton collects it separately, at City Hall, 1009 Main Street (270-527-8677). The city's page says not to use its link for Marshall County taxes.

faqs.q: What was the Marshall County discount for 2026 bills?
faqs.a: Two percent on payments from November 1 through November 30, 2026, under the schedule the Sheriff's Office announced. Face amount applied through December 2026.

faqs.q: Which Marshall County office collects delinquent taxes?
faqs.a: The County Clerk, at 1101 Main Street in Benton. The Department of Revenue says interest of one percent a month starts once bills reach the clerk.

faqs.q: What is the Marshall County homestead exemption worth?
faqs.a: $49,100 off assessed value for the 2025 and 2026 assessment years, for owners who are 65 or older or totally disabled and who apply at the PVA.
